title: Why heat speeds up reactions
body: For particles to react, they have to collide, and hit hard enough to break their old bonds. That minimum energy is called the activation energy. Most collisions are too gentle, and nothing happens.
In hot water the particles move faster. They collide more often, and far more of those collisions have enough energy to react. So the reaction runs faster.
A handy rule of thumb: for many reactions near room temperature, every 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate. That's why a fizzy tablet in hot water is finished long before one in cold water.
realWorld: Fridges keep food fresh by slowing down the reactions that make it go off. Cooking does the opposite: heat speeds up the reactions that change raw food.
